newsitem.title: MEXICO: INSTANT VIEW - Televisa deal furrows brows.
newsitem.headline: INSTANT VIEW - Televisa deal furrows brows.

text.p: Analysts said Friday that Mexican media giant Televisa probably would have benefitted more from an all-cash deal in the sale of its stake in PanAmSat Corp than from the cash and equity stake it will receive.
"The company would have preferred all cash," said Felix Boni, director of research at HSBC James Capel in Mexico City. "They certainly needed the cash."
Televisa announced earlier Friday that it expects to receive about $600 million in cash and an equity interest of about 8.5 percent in a new venture between PanAmSat and Hughes Electronics Corp.
PanAmSat, in which Televisa sold its 40.5 percent stake, also announced earlier an accord to merge its satellite services operations with Hughes Electronics Corp.
Boni said he was still pouring over the details of the deal and added that, despite the company's debt burden, Televisa had taken a forward-looking stance on its PanAmSat holding.
"It is a company (PanAmSat) that has a promising future in a promising industry," he said of the new satellite broadcasting venture.
Despite analyst head-scratching, Televisa ADRs in New York were up 1/8 to 29-7/8 in early trading. On the Mexican stock exchange, Televisa's benchmark CPO shares were up 50 centavos to 113 pesos.

In an overnight report, Mexican brokerage Valores Finamex had forecast that Televisa could have received up to $1.215 billion in cash in the deal, adding weight to the market feeling that Televisa came out of the deal a little cash light.

"It is clear that Televisa's objective is to realise the full 100 percent of its investment in cash so as to be able to repay its peso debt with Banamex of around 3.4 billion pesos, and to use the rest to purchase programming for its DTH venture in Latin America and Spain and Portugal," Finamex said in its report prior to the announcement.
Banamex is Mexico's largest bank and the main unit of the financial company Grupo Financiero Banamex-Accival.

Shayne McGuire, Televisa analyst with Deutsche Morgan Grenfell in Mexico City, said what he found unexpected about the deal was the length of time it will take for the company to receive the cash payment.
"It is going to take six to 12 months. It was not expected to take that long and that is probably one of the reasons the stock (price) is not reacting too positively," McGuire said.

"I think it's a pretty attractive package for Televisa," one New York analyst said. "Televisa wanted cash for this, but all things considered it would have been a $3 billion deal and nobody has that kind of money lying around. My belief is this is the most cash that Televisa was able to get."
The analyst's $3 billion figure referred to the total value of PanAmSat, not just Televisa's holding.
Televisa bought its stake in PanAmSat for $200 million in 1992. Today its 40.5 million shares of PanAmSat stock are worth about $1.2 billion, according to analyst calculations.
"The cash that Hughes was able to bring to the table was pretty much instrumental," he said.
